scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Four-Year Album Gap Explanation (1992-1996)
podcast.body: The significant four-year delay between Rage Against the Machine's debut album and their second record, Evil Empire, was attributed to three main factors: extensive touring, side projects (like recording movie soundtracks), and internal political dissension. This delay was unusual for a band whose debut was considered a "game changer," as maintaining momentum typically required a second album within 18 months. "First they toured and toured and toured. Second they got sidetracked on some non-album projects like recording songs for movie soundtracks. And third, internal politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Second Stage Act
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine was among the bands featured on the second stage at selected dates during the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, which boasted a critically acclaimed lineup. "You could have seen the stone type of pilots rage against the machine, Cypress Hill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career Momentum and Perception (1993)
podcast.body: After their Lollapalooza 1993 performance, Rage Against the Machine was perceived as a "new, young, angry band" whose debut album and live reaction indicated they were "destined to be the biggest band in the world." However, this potential did not fully materialize as expected due to various internal and external challenges. "Their debut album was so good and the reaction to what they played and said and performed was so positive that it seemed that they were just destined to be the biggest band in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Attempt to Record Second Album in Atlanta (1994)
podcast.body: In late 1994, Rage Against the Machine attempted to record their second album in Atlanta, where they moved into a house, jammed, and wrote 20 songs over four to five months. This effort was "aborted" due to escalating tensions and creative differences. During this period, they also fired their manager, reportedly because he "wasn't buying into the revolution." "They wrote 20 songs over the four or five months that they stayed in Atlanta, but tensions and creative differences got so crazy that everything was aborted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Crow Soundtrack Contribution (1994)
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine contributed to *The Crow* soundtrack in 1994, which was released at the peak of the alternative and Lollapalooza period. The film's music supervisors successfully curated a dark and fitting collection that reflected the movie's themes and its tragic production history. "They got the cure and rage against the machine, and Jesus and Mary Chain and the violent foms."

podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine contributed music to the soundtrack for the movie "The Crow," released at the end of March 1994, which was noted as one of the best soundtracks of the decade. podcast.title: Saturday Night Live Incident (1996)
podcast.body: During a performance on Saturday Night Live, Rage Against the Machine protested guest host Steve Forbes, a billionaire Republican presidential candidate, by hanging an American flag upside down as a sign of disrespect. They were only allowed to play one song and were swiftly escorted from the building. It was rumored that Zach de la Rocha intended to publicly denounce General Electric (NBC's parent company) as a manufacturer of weapons and perpetrator of war crimes during the First Gulf War. The band subsequently accused GE and NBC of censorship. "Rage didn't get a chance to play a second on that night because he was rumored that Zach was going to call out General Electric, the parent company of NBC, as manufacturers of weapons and perpetrators of war crimes in the first Gulf War."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Coachella 1999 Payment Delay
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine was one of several bands approached by Coachella organizers after the disastrous 1999 festival, asking them to wait a little while before they could be paid due to significant financial losses. "The promoter lost close to a million dollars, and they actually had to go back to several of the bands like Toul and Rage and said, could you wait a little while before we pay you out?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Matrix Soundtrack Contribution (1999)
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine was featured on the first *Matrix* soundtrack, released in 1999. The album was characterized by "really cool heavy stuff," including contributions from other heavy acts like Marilyn Manson, Ministry, The Prodigy, and Rammstein. "It was some really cool heavy stuff, Marilyn Manson, Ministry of the Prodigy, Ramstein, Rage Against the Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 2000 Breakup
podcast.body: Rage Against The Machine broke up around the year 2000, contributing to a sense of disappointment and decline within the rock and alt-rock scenes at the turn of the millennium. "There were other disappointments too, rage against the machine broke up."

podcast.title: Breakup Date (October 18, 2000)

podcast.title: Implosion (October 18, 2000) – Zack de la Rocha's Departure
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine experienced an "implosion" on October 18, 2000, when their singer, Zack de la Rocha, quit the band. Despite this, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, and Brad Wilk—decided to stay together and search for a new vocalist, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "Singer and Zacti La Roca quit the band on October 18, 2000, and frankly, that was fine as far as the other three guys were concerned. They planned to stay together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rhyme and Reason Tour Cancellation (2000)
podcast.body: In the summer of 2000, Rage Against the Machine planned a 30-date "Rhyme and Reason Tour" with the Beastie Boys, featuring activist messages and a promise to donate a dollar from every ticket to charity. However, the tour was entirely canceled after Beastie Boys member Mike D dislocated his shoulder in a mountain bike accident, rendering him unable to perform. "But then Mike D drove his mountain bike into a pothole and dislocated his shoulder. Turned out to be so bad that the whole tour had to be canceled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Zach de la Rocha's Departure and Band Breakup (2000)
podcast.body: On October 18, 2000, Zach de la Rocha announced his departure from Rage Against the Machine, stating that the band's "decision-making process has completely failed" and no longer met the collective aspirations or his "artistic and political ideal." His exit marked the end of the band's initial run, attributed to the toll taken by competing philosophies and ideologies within the group. "On October 18th, 2000, Zach D. LaRocca released a statement, I feel that it is now necessary to leave Rage because our decision-making process has completely failed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Zack de la Rocha Quits (2000)
podcast.body: On October 18, 2000, Zack de la Rocha quit the band, citing a "completely failed" decision-making process that "no longer meaning the aspirations of all four of us collectively as a band, and from my perspective has undermined our artistic and political ideal." This was broadly understood as political and creative differences, which extended to minor disputes like the color of merchandise t-shirts. "It was necessary to leave Rage because our decision-making process has completely failed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Zack de la Rocha's Departure and Return (2000, 2007)
podcast.body: Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine in the fall of 2000 to pursue solo work, but faced challenges finding inspiration for a full album. The band later reunited in 2007 and has continued to perform through a series of live gigs, demonstrating their enduring presence despite de la Rocha's earlier departure. "When Zach De La Roca left Raging Against the Machine in the fall of 2000, it was almost a given that he would move on to some kind of solo work. He did. But then he kind of got lost. It all worked out well, though. Rage got back to you there in 2007 and had been holding it together through a series of live gigs ever since."

podcast.title: Reunion for Coachella (2007) Driven by George Bush
podcast.body: Despite significant animosity rumored between Zach de la Rocha and the other band members, and numerous rejected offers for reunion, Rage Against the Machine eventually reunited for the Coachella Music Festival in April 2007, following rumors in late 2006. According to Tom Morello, the catalyst for their reunion was the political climate under President George Bush, as the band felt compelled to "stand up and oppose what was going on with the U.S. domestically and internationally." "Well according to Tom Morello, it was George Bush. The time had simply come for a band like Rage to stand up and oppose what was going on with the U.S. domestically and internationally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion with Zack de la Rocha (2007)
podcast.body: After their project with Chris Cornell (Audioslave) ended, Rage Against the Machine reunited with Zack de la Rocha, a reunion that has continued intermittently since 2007. "And then there was a Rage reunion with Zach, something that has persisted off and on since 2007."

podcast.title: Studio Re-recording with Springsteen (2014)
podcast.body: Tom Morello was featured on a studio re-recording of "The Ghost of Tom Joad" that appeared on Bruce Springsteen's 2014 album, "High Hopes," underscoring the mutual admiration and collaboration between the two artists. "And if you look on Springsteen's 2014 album High Hopes, there is a studio re-recording that features Tom Morello."

podcast.title: 2022 Reunion Tour Cut Short
podcast.body: The band embarked on a reunion tour in 2022, which lasted only 36 days, from July 9, 2022, in Troy, Wisconsin, to August 14, 2022, at Madison Square Garden. The tour was cut short after vocalist Zach D. LaRocca tore his Achilles tendon on stage. "Although their reunion lasted all of 36 days before it fell apart, the first show July 9, 2022 in Troy, Wisconsin, last show, August 14, 2022 at Madison Square Garden. It might have gone on longer and might have been much bigger. Ted Singer, Zach D. LaRocca, not torn his Achilles on stage."

podcast.title: "Arm the Homeless Electric" Guitar
podcast.body: His most famous guitar is a custom instrument called the "Arm the Homeless Electric," a slogan he carved into its body in the early 1990s. He purchased the wood body from a luthier in Hollywood in 1986, then customized all its components to his liking, making it his main guitar except during his Audioslave period. "His most famous is probably a custom job that he calls his Arm the Homeless Electric. He calls it this because he carved that slogan, Arm the Homeless, into the body of a guitar sometime in the early 1990s."

podcast.title: "Evil Empire" Cover Art Interpretation
podcast.body: Zack de la Rocha of Rage Against the Machine provided an interpretation of the boy's expression on the "Evil Empire" album cover, a painting by Mel Ramos. He stated that the boy's smile is a facade, projecting control within the power structure of the United States, but upon deeper examination, the boy is actually "very, very afraid." "Zach D'Auroraka says it's all about the power structure in the United States. He's smiling because he wants to project that he's in control."

podcast.title: 21st Century Reunion
podcast.body: Rage Against The Machine was mentioned as one of the prominent alt-rock bands that reunited in the 21st century, helping to inject temporary vitality back into the alt-rock scene and bring lapsed fans back. "In addition, the Pixies, smashing pumpkins, the lemon heads, rage against the machine...These reunions injected some life into the scene, albeit temporary life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Advocacy and Support for Causes
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine consistently engaged in political activism, playing benefits and political rallies, and supporting various causes. These included the case of Mumia Abu-Jamal, a journalist on death row for a 1982 murder of a police officer in Philadelphia, and participating in the first Tibetan Freedom Festival, organized by the Beastie Boys. "This included the case of Mumaia Abu Jamal, a journalist who was on death row for killing a cop in Philadelphia in 1982, and included the first Tibetan Freedom Festival, which was organized by the Beastie Boys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Album Title's Political Context
podcast.body: The title "Evil Empire" for Rage Against the Machine's 1996 album directly appropriates a phrase from a Ronald Reagan speech, which he used to describe the Soviet Union. However, the band explicitly intended to apply this label to the United States, reflecting their strong political stance and criticism of American power structures. "But given Rage's politics, they meant for it to apply to the United States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Anti-System Message and Name Origin
podcast.body: Their message was profoundly different from contemporary music, expressing raw anger towards the world and the established system. The band's name, "Rage Against the Machine," encapsulates this philosophy, with "machine" directly referring to the political system. "El mensaje de Richard Gensemason era totalmente y radicalmente distinto a todo lo que se estaba haciendo. Y ellos mostraban esa rabia hacia el mundo, hacia el sistema, era una lucha combativa, era todo de ellos hacia afuera. De hecho, ya viene el nombre porque Richard Gensemason es la furia contra el sistema, o sea, es máquina, pero máquina viene a referirse al sistema que tenía el sistema político."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Poniendo en su lugar a Rage Against the Machine

podcast.title: Band Formation and Political Stance
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine formed after finding members through musicians-wanted classified ads. Over eight years, they earned a reputation as one of the most political and funkiest bands in the alternative nation, largely due to the contributions of Tim Commerford and Brad Wilk. "Over the next eight years rage against the machine got a rep as one of the most political bands in the alternative nation and one of the funkiest thanks to Tim Bob and Brad Wilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Naming
podcast.body: The band adopted the name "Rage Against The Machine" from the title of a planned second album by Zach Dela Roka's previous band, Inside Out, which never materialized. The name was ultimately deemed more fitting and powerful for the new group. "the band had decided that Rage against the machine would be a great name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band's Political Nature and Internal Dissension
podcast.body: As a "highly political, super socially conscious band," Rage Against the Machine was seen as more than just a musical group, but a "political unit" aiming for "political, social and economic change." While their goals were admirable and standards high, the difficulty in achieving global change led to internal disillusionment and dissension, contributing to creative differences and tensions. "See here's a problem with a highly political, super socially conscious band like rage. You're more than just a band. You're a political unit using the system to drive political, social and economic change."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brad Wilk's Background and Influences
podcast.body: Brad Wilk, originally from Chicago, started out as a guitarist before becoming a fan of The Who's drummer, Keith Moon. He pursued jazz drumming lessons from serious pros, idolizing Elvin Jones, from whom he learned funky grooves. He also studied James Brown and George Clinton records, mastering the technique of inserting a microsecond delay into his timekeeping, crucial for a good groove. "He also studied James Brown and George Clinton records and learned how to insert a microsecond delay into his time keeping something that's essential to a good groove."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Cornell Suggestion
podcast.body: In 2001, producer Rick Rubin suggested the band approach Chris Cornell, noting Soundgarden wasn't reuniting and Cornell's solo work lacked traction. A meeting in May 2001 led to instant chemistry, resulting in 21 songs written over 19 days. "At some point in 2001, producer Rick Rubin said, you know, sound garden isn't getting back together. Chris Cardell's solo work is okay, but it hasn't gained him any traction. Why don't ask him if he wants to join forces?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Confrontational Lyrics
podcast.body: The band's lyrics were characterized by their strength, impact, and combative nature, directly challenging the entire system. They conveyed messages against capitalism, globalization, the political system, money, and banks, urging listeners to channel their sadness into anger and fight against societal oppression. "Las letras de rechagan semacín eran realmente fuertes, impactantes y combatientes contra todo el sistema. Hay mensajes anticapitalistas, hay mensajes anticlobalización, hay mensajes en contra del sistema político, en contra del dinero, en contra de los bancos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Poniendo en su lugar a Rage Against the Machine

podcast.title: Contradiction with Major Record Label
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine faced an "inherent contradiction" by being a left-wing collective while operating under a "multinational major record label." This arrangement created tension, as the band was expected to fulfill contractual obligations like touring, promotion, interviews, and MTV appearances, which often included editing out expletives from singles for radio and video play. "Complicating matters was the fact that they were a left-wing collective working for a multinational major record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creative/Political Dispute Leading to Singer's Departure
podcast.body: Singer Zack de la Rocha left the band due to a "creative dispute, maybe a political dispute," as he sought to take the band in a direction that the other members did not agree with. "Zach, Rage's singer, had decided to leave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decision to Continue as a Unit
podcast.body: Following Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Timmy, and Brad—decided they wanted to stay together and continue making music. "However, the other three guys, Tom, Timmy and Brad, decided that they really wanted to stay together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dreadlocks in 1990s Rock and Metal
podcast.body: Zack de la Rocha, from Rage Against the Machine, was one of the prominent figures in the 1990s music scene to adopt dreadlocks, showcasing the style's widespread appeal across genres. "And then through the 90s, dreads appeared on everyone from Rob Zombie and Zach from Raging Us the Machine to Jonathan Davis of Corn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Guitar Start and Band Experience
podcast.body: Tom Morello picked up a cheap Japanese K guitar at age 13 for about $100, and within weeks he was playing in a Led Zeppelin cover band. He began seriously studying the guitar around age 20. "Tom first picked up a guitar at age 13, a K guitar, a cheapo Japanese thing that cost about 100 bucks. And within weeks he was playing in a Led Zeppelin cover band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Future Recording Potential
podcast.body: Despite the band's current focus on live gigs and activism without new recordings, the possibility of future material is left open. The idea is posed that if "circumstances are right" and they feel a need to deliver a new message, they might record again, though the value of preserving their legacy of three "influential and revolutionary" studio albums is also considered. "If circumstances are right and they feel they need to get together to deliver a new message, I can see them doing it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Harvard Attendance with Gibson Explorer
podcast.body: He took his Gibson Explorer with him when he enrolled at Harvard University and still owns the instrument. "And this Gibson Explorer was the guitar he took with him when he enrolled in Harvard. He still has him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: High Guitar Position for Maneuverability
podcast.body: Morello deliberately holds his guitar high on his body, providing more room to move his hands along the strings and create unusual sounds on the guitar's body and fretboard. "He plays it way up high on the body. And that's done deliberately because it gives him more room to move his hands up and down the strings and to create all sorts of unusual sounds on the body of the guitar and the fretboard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hip Hop and "Scratching" Guitar Technique
podcast.body: Influenced by hip hop and rap acts like Public Enemy and Run DMC, he developed a unique technique of "scratching" his guitar strings, mimicking a DJ on a turntable. "He got deeper into hip hop and rap, public enemy and run DMC were big influences, which also moved him to start scratching his guitar strings like a DJ wood on a turntable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Fishbone
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine is among the bands that have cited Fishbone as an important influence on their music. "Rage Against The Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Living Color
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine was inspired by Living Color, who are noted for their fusion of funk and metal. "another band that inspired groups like Rage Against the Machine, and Limbiscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Subsequent Music
podcast.body: While their specific political and protest content didn't widely establish a direct "school" of anti-system rock, Rage Against the Machine's musical style significantly influenced bands like Linkin Park and Limp Bizkit, contributing to a "hardcore punk hip hop" subgenre. More importantly, RATM helped redirect rock's trajectory, inspiring bands such as Pearl Jam to move beyond introspective sentiments towards more outward-facing social and political messages. "Si sentaron un poco una nueva variante del rock, sería ese hardcore punk, un poco hip hop, un tanto fuerte y rudo, que después nos traería bandas, como Linkin Park, o como Limp Biscuit...pero que proses gracias a toda esa estela, perdí el enorme contenido político y de protesta que tenía rechagan semacín, se centraba mucho en las formas pero no en el fondo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Poniendo en su lugar a Rage Against the Machine

podcast.title: Initial Name Retention
podcast.body: Initially, the new project with Chris Cornell was still intended to be called Rage Against the Machine. A bootleg CD with this title and featuring Chris Cornell exists, but Cornell's style diverged too much from the original Rage sound, prompting the band to reconsider the name. "In fact, I have a bootleg CD in my collection entitled Rage Against the Machine Feature in Chris Cornell."

podcast.title: Initial Performances and Demo Tape
podcast.body: After forming, the band began by playing at parties and small clubs throughout the Los Angeles area. They self-funded the recording of an indie cassette demo, which they then sold directly at their shows to build a following. "So the new groups started playing parties and small clubs in and around the LA area."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Liner Notes Thank Yous
podcast.body: The debut album's liner notes feature an extensive list of acknowledgments, including Beto (Zach Dela Roka's father, an artist who destroyed his paintings during a nervous breakdown) and revolutionary musicians such as Chuck D and Joe Strummer. "Beto is Zack's dad, the artist who went crazy in Burdala's paintings."

podcast.title: Major Label Deal (Epic Records)
podcast.body: Despite previous negative experiences with major labels by three-quarters of the band members, Rage Against The Machine signed with Epic Records. This decision was driven by the label's agreement to grant the band complete creative control over their material and recognizing that a major label's global distribution and marketing power was essential for effectively disseminating their political message. "Epic was the major that agreed to all of Rage's demands."

podcast.title: Meeting Subcomandante Marcos in the Mayan Jungle
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine accepted an invitation from the Zapatistas, a Libertarian Marxist group led by Subcomandante Marcos, who had declared war on the Mexican government in 1994 and used the internet to reach out to like-minded left-wing bands. Despite some media portraying the Zapatistas as terrorists, Rage met with their leader in the Mayan jungle, simultaneously condemning American politicians and military personnel as war criminals, showcasing their "very bold, very confrontational stuff." "While certain elements of the media portrayed the Zapatistas as terrorists, there was Rage Against the Machine, meeting with Subcomundente Marcos in the Mayan jungle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: NBC Blacklisting
podcast.body: Following the controversial Saturday Night Live incident, Rage Against the Machine faced an absolute censorship and a complete ban from the entire NBC communication group. Despite these severe repercussions, the band steadfastly defended their actions, demonstrating their unwavering commitment to their principles. "A partir de ahí ya vendría la censura absoluta y el absoluto borrado de rechagan semacín dentro de todo el grupo de comunicación de la NBC pero ellos al final hasta sus últimas consecuencias defendían esa manera de actuar."

podcast.title: Post-Reunion Activities and No New Albums
podcast.body: Since their 2007 reunion, Rage Against the Machine has toured, engaged in "rabble rousing at various political conventions," and generally continued "stirring the pot" regarding political issues. However, there has been no indication that the band plans to record any new studio albums together, primarily focusing on live performances and activism. "However, there were never any indications that there would be a new album."

podcast.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining three members wanted to stay together. They briefly considered becoming the backing band for Ozzy Osbourne or working with Macy Gray. podcast.title: Powerful Bottom End
podcast.body: A key element contributing to Rage Against the Machine's distinct sound was their powerful "bottom end," driven by bassist Tim Commerford and drummer Brad Wilk. Singer Zack de la Rocha and guitarist Tom Morello recognized the need to allow the rhythm section ample space to contribute to the band's overall sound. podcast.title: Rage's Lifespan Aligns with Don Letts' Theory
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine formed in 1991 and broke up in 2000, lasting approximately nine years. This timeframe aligns with British DJ and filmmaker Don Letts' theory that the average lifespan of most bands is seven to nine years, after which they typically "explode" due to internal pressures like creative differences and diverging lifestyles. "They formed in 1991, got big real fast, and right on schedule, they broke up in 2000, torn apart by a series of internal conflicts."

podcast.body: After the failed Atlanta sessions, the band relocated to California to cool off. They then developed new songs in Hollywood, which were subsequently recorded in Melbourne, Australia, for their second album, Evil Empire. podcast.title: Relevance to Generation X
podcast.body: Rage Against the Machine's powerful anti-capitalist, anti-system, and anti-globalization message deeply resonated with Generation X, who felt like "prisoners of the system." This generation, having grown up in perceived economic prosperity, found themselves lacking a future, overlooked, and unable to partake in the world's wealth. "Mucha gente se sintió mucho mejor identificada con ese discurso, porque al final dos 80 habían sido una etapa de mucha prosperidad económica...Y a primeros de los 90...empezaba a ver la generación perdida, la generación X...que se encuentran que el mundo no les ofrece un futuro, los deja como delado, atascados y viven en un mundo próspero del que ellos no pueden formar aparte."

podcast.title: Tim Commerford's Background and Influences

His mother was a mathematician and his father an aeronautical engineer who worked on the space shuttle. He and Zack de la Rocha formed their first band, Juvenile Expression, in grade seven, after Zack taught Tim to play bass using the Sex Pistols' "Never Mind the Bollocks" album. podcast.title: Tom Morello's Guitar Style
podcast.body: By the release of The Battle of Los Angeles, Tom Morello had developed a highly unique guitar playing style. He was known for using numerous effects to create diverse sounds, but a key characteristic highlighted was "the space between the notes," where "short gaps of nothing between the notes often say more than riffs that don't have gaps," creating a powerful effect. "By this time, he had developed a very unique playing style. He used lots of effects to get lots of different sounds. But when you listen to Tom's playing, the thing that really gets me is the space between the notes."

podcast.title: Tom Morello's Songwriting Philosophy
podcast.body: In an interview with Alternative Press magazine, Tom Morello articulated his view on songwriting, stating his disinterest in merely "good songs" that prompt toe-tapping. He aimed to write "great songs" that could "destroy cops and set fire to the suburbs," reflecting the band's confrontational political stance. "A good song should make you want to tap your toes and get with your girl. A great song should destroy cops and set fire to the suburbs. I'm only interested in writing great songs."

podcast.title: Tony Iommi's Influence on Restraint

Some police departments sought to block gigs due to fears of "civil insurrection and violence and riots." "This combination scared certain law enforcement authorities along the itinerary, which created more difficulties."

The presence of such bands contributed to a pervasive atmosphere of "male rage and testosterone" that ultimately fueled the frustration, hatred, and subsequent violence among the festival's 200,000 attendees. podcast.title: Zach de la Rocha's Fan Engagement and Disillusionment
podcast.body: Zach de la Rocha often cultivated strong relationships with fans by holding political discussions in venue parking lots after shows with groups of kids. However, he felt disillusioned when only a small fraction (e.g., 15 kids out of a 5,000-person crowd) stayed, questioning if their political message was truly getting through or if fans were merely pretending to engage. "For example, it was an uncommon to find Zach D. Leroka in the parking lot of the venue after the show holding a political discussion with 15 kids."

podcast.title: Zach de la Rocha's Unsuccessful Solo Sessions
podcast.body: After Rage's breakup, Zach de la Rocha attempted solo projects. He worked with DJ Shadow on a planned "silhouette" project that never materialized. Later, sessions with Trent Reznor were also unsuccessful, with Reznor stating, "those tapes will never see the light of day." Although a few of Zach's songs were eventually released, a full solo album never emerged from these efforts. "He worked with DJ Shadow with the hopes of making a silhouette, but that didn't work. Then he hooked up with Trent Rezner. But those sessions were a disaster too."

xref.title: Joe Hill (1915) – Swedish IWW Songwriter, Coined "Pie in the Sky," Executed by Firing Squad; Father of the Modern Protest Song
xref.body: Joe Hill was a Swedish-born itinerant laborer and songwriter for the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), a socialist union founded in Chicago in 1905 that organized logging, mining, farm, and factory workers. Hill is credited with coining the phrase "Pie in the Sky." He was arrested and charged with the murder of two people in Salt Lake City, subject to a major media trial, found guilty, and executed by firing squad on November 19, 1915. He is considered the father of the modern protest song and has many fans in the rock world, including Tom Morello of Rage Against the Machine, who has organized a memorial in Joe's name, performed his songs, and released songs about him. "You can draw a straight line from Rage Against the Machine right back to the 1910s and Joe Hill."

xref.body: Fishbone holds a fanatical following and is cited as an important influence by a long list of bands, including Sublime, 311, Goldfinger, Rage Against the Machine, and Faith No More. "No doubt. Sublime. 311. Goldfinger. Rage Against The Machine. Faith No More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Name Retention
xref.body: Initially, the new project with Chris Cornell was still intended to be called Rage Against the Machine. A bootleg CD with this title and featuring Chris Cornell exists, but Cornell's style diverged too much from the original Rage sound, prompting the band to reconsider the name. "In fact, I have a bootleg CD in my collection entitled Rage Against the Machine Feature in Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initiated Audioslave Formation
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure from Rage Against The Machine, Tom Morello contacted Chris Cornell to see if he would be interested in joining the remaining members of the band (Timmy and Brad). "On the other end was guitarist Tom Morello from Rage Against The Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joining Rage Against The Machine (unofficially)
xref.body: Cornell was contacted by Tom Morello after Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against The Machine. He joined Morello, Timmy, and Brad, and they convened to write songs, which "worked out really well." A bootleg recording from this period exists, labeled "Rage Against The Machine, both Chris Cornell and Vocals. Tom Morello on the line." "Now Chris thought this sounded pretty good, so they convened to write some songs. That worked out really well. And Chris joined Rage Against The Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Legendary Canadian Producer
xref.body: Jack Richardson is recognized as a legendary Canadian producer who was responsible for producing "all the guess who's best records." He is also the father of Garth Richardson, who produced Rage Against The Machine's debut album. "Jack did all the guess who's best records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Major Label Deal (Epic Records)
xref.body: Despite previous negative experiences with major labels by three-quarters of the band members, Rage Against The Machine signed with Epic Records. This decision was driven by the label's agreement to grant the band complete creative control over their material and recognizing that a major label's global distribution and marketing power was essential for effectively disseminating their political message. "Epic was the major that agreed to all of Rage's demands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meeting Subcomandante Marcos in the Mayan Jungle
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine accepted an invitation from the Zapatistas, a Libertarian Marxist group led by Subcomandante Marcos, who had declared war on the Mexican government in 1994 and used the internet to reach out to like-minded left-wing bands. Despite some media portraying the Zapatistas as terrorists, Rage met with their leader in the Mayan jungle, simultaneously condemning American politicians and military personnel as war criminals, showcasing their "very bold, very confrontational stuff." "While certain elements of the media portrayed the Zapatistas as terrorists, there was Rage Against the Machine, meeting with Subcomundente Marcos in the Mayan jungle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Chuck D, identified as both a musician and revolutionary, received "props" in the liner notes of Rage Against The Machine's debut album. "Revolutionaries and musicians like Chuck D and Joe Stromer get props."

"This is a punk rap group from Newark, New Jersey. They're very much into the same headspace as Rage, two guys, the OGM and Yeti 999."

xref.body: The Beastie Boys were responsible for organizing the first Tibetan Freedom Festival, an event that Rage Against the Machine supported and participated in as part of their broader activism. "included the first Tibetan Freedom Festival, which was organized by the Beastie Boys."

xref.title: Pez - Rage Against The Machine Comparison
xref.body: When Ben Kowalewicz left his radio job to pursue the band, his then-boss, Phil Evans, described the band as being "kind of like Rage Against The Machine." "Yeah, he's got this band that, you know, they're kind of like rage against the machine."

xref.title: Post-Reunion Activities and No New Albums
xref.body: Since their 2007 reunion, Rage Against the Machine has toured, engaged in "rabble rousing at various political conventions," and generally continued "stirring the pot" regarding political issues. However, there has been no indication that the band plans to record any new studio albums together, primarily focusing on live performances and activism. "However, there were never any indications that there would be a new album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Powerful Bottom End
xref.body: A key element contributing to Rage Against the Machine's distinct sound was their powerful "bottom end," driven by bassist Tim Commerford and drummer Brad Wilk. Singer Zack de la Rocha and guitarist Tom Morello recognized the need to allow the rhythm section ample space to contribute to the band's overall sound. "One of the things that made Rage Against the Machine so cool was that bottom end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-Pearl Jam Jobs and Bands
xref.body: Before moving from San Diego to Seattle to join Pearl Jam, Eddie Vedder moved from Chicago to San Diego where he worked booking bands in a club, security at a hotel, and at a gas station, alongside his passion for surfing. He was involved in several bands, including The Butts, Surf and Destroy, and Indian Style (featuring future Rage Against the Machine drummer Brad Wilk), with Bad Radio showing the most promise. "When Eddie Vetter moved from Chicago to San Diego, he got a job booking bands in a club. He also worked security at a hotel. He worked at a gas station and he spent a lot of time surfing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Predecessor to Audioslave
xref.body: Soundgarden is identified as one of the two "previous incarnations" that Audioslave embodied. The flame sculpture on Audioslave's debut album cover explicitly symbolizes "the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine." "The flame is the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance, embodying the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine."

xref.title: Producer Brendan O'Brien's Work
xref.body: Brendan O'Brien, who produced Billy Talent's third album, was highly regarded by the band for having produced "all our favorite Rage Against the Machine records," which was a significant factor in their decision to work with him. "Brenner O'Brien he's done all our favorite rage against machine records and Pearl Jam record."

xref.body: Prophets of Rage is considered another iteration of Rage Against the Machine, featuring its instrumental members alongside Chuck D of Public Enemy and B-Real of Cypress Hill, effectively replacing Zack de la Rocha. "And then there's Prophets of Rage, of course, which could be looked at as yet another iteration of Rage Against the Machine with Chuck D and B. Real and place him Zach."

xref.title: Rage Against the Machine with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Audioslave was essentially the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) with Chris Cornell as the new frontman, resulting in a significant musical "makeover" from their original sound. "Audio Slave, which, let's be honest, is really Rage Against the Machine with a big Chris Cornell makeover."

xref.title: Rage's Lifespan Aligns with Don Letts' Theory
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine formed in 1991 and broke up in 2000, lasting approximately nine years. This timeframe aligns with British DJ and filmmaker Don Letts' theory that the average lifespan of most bands is seven to nine years, after which they typically "explode" due to internal pressures like creative differences and diverging lifestyles. "They formed in 1991, got big real fast, and right on schedule, they broke up in 2000, torn apart by a series of internal conflicts."

xref.title: Refusal to Reunite for Recording
xref.body: The Smiths are mentioned as an example of a band, similar to The Clash and The Stone Roses, that despite significant offers, did not get back together to record new music after their initial run. This comparison is made in the context of Rage Against the Machine's decision not to record new material after their reunion. "Same with the Smiths... If they all did try to get back together and make the same kind of music they did when they were young angry men, what would the results be?"

This serves as a parallel to Rage Against the Machine's post-reunion stance on new recordings. "Same with the Stone Roses. If they all did try to get back together and make the same kind of music they did when they were young angry men, what would the results be?"

xref.title: Search for New Singer – Auditions and Rick Rubin's Role
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine auditioned several potential vocalists, including Be-Real of Cypress Hill, but none seemed to fit. Producer Rick Rubin eventually suggested Chris Cornell, which proved to be a pivotal recommendation, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "They auditioned a bunch of people, including Be Real of Cypress Hill, but nothing really worked. Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Socially Conscious and Politically Active
xref.body: Despite differences in musical sound, Rage Against the Machine and Bruce Springsteen are described as "kindred spirits" due to their shared commitment to being socially conscious, giving a voice to the voiceless, and engaging in political activism. "Despite the differences in the sound of their music, they are definitely kindred spirits when it comes to being socially conscious, giving voice to the voiceless, and engaging in political activism."

xref.title: Solo Album with Trent Reznor - Unreleased
xref.body: After Rage Against the Machine disbanded in 2000, Zack De La Rocha began working on a solo record, delving into hip hop and freestyle rapping. He collaborated with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Reznor, who produced the material. Despite the material being considered "good" by Reznor, the album was never released and was shelved indefinitely for unknown reasons. "Rage was done by 2000... But Zach was determined to go solo. He got deep into hip hop and freestyle rapping and started working with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Rosner on a solo record. The material was good too, according to Trent anyway. But for a recent still unknown, the album was never released, shelved forever."

xref.title: Stylistic Contrast for "45"
xref.body: Sum 41's song "45" is explicitly contrasted by Derek Whibley with the style of Rage Against the Machine, clarifying that "45" is not a "rage against a machine song" that calls out specific policies or aims to change opinions, but rather expresses personal frustration. "It's more saying, you're just not my kind of guy. But I'm not really, it's not like a rage against a machine song."

xref.title: Support from Tool
xref.body: Rage Against The Machine gained significant early exposure by opening for Tool at some of their concerts. Adam Jones of Tool, a friend of Tom Morello, invited Rage to perform, which helped their demo tape attract the attention of talent scouts and led to a bidding war. "Adam invited Rage to open for some of their gigs."

xref.title: Symbolism of "Audioslave" Album Cover
xref.body: Storm Thorgerson, designer of Audioslave's 2002 debut album cover, explained its profound symbolism. Set on the volcanic island of Lanzarote, the large metal sculpture resembling flames represents "the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance," embodying the collective memory of the band's two previous incarnations, Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine. The solitary figure in the landscape represents "pilgrims or slaves of sound." "The flame is the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance, embodying the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine."

xref.title: Tom Morello's Solo Project
xref.body: Following the dissolution of Rage Against the Machine and while Audioslave was active, Tom Morello began performing solo under the name The Night Watchman. His performances were described as "low-key open mic nights, Billy Bragg style," featuring just him, a guitar, and an amp. "It began performing low-key open mic nights, Billy Bragg style, just him, a guitar and an amp under the name The Night Watchmen."

xref.title: Tour with Wu-Tang Clan and Law Enforcement Issues
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine's decision to tour with the "very political hip-hop outfit" Wu-Tang Clan caused alarm among law enforcement authorities. Some police departments sought to block gigs due to fears of "civil insurrection and violence and riots." Additionally, the two groups eventually realized their politics were not fully aligned, leading to rumors of a backstage fight. "This combination scared certain law enforcement authorities along the itinerary, which created more difficulties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Audioslave
xref.body: After Chris Cornell joined the remaining members of Rage Against The Machine, they collectively decided to "jettison the Rage name" and reform as Audioslave. "And I'm not really sure why there was a collective decision to jettison the Rage name in favor of Audio Slive, which is where we are today."

xref.title: Unique Genre Fusion
xref.body: Brass Against, featuring vocalist Sophia Urista, is described as the "love child" of Rage Against the Machine and an old school brass band, indicating a unique blend of powerful rock with traditional brass elements. "Speaking of covers, there's Sophia Irista and Brass Against. They've been described as the love channel of Rage Against the Machine and some kind of old school brass band."

xref.title: Unreleased Collaboration with Trent Reznor
xref.body: After leaving Rage Against the Machine, Zack de la Rocha attempted a collaboration with Trent Reznor, which reportedly yielded up to 20 tracks. However, this project was never released, with de la Rocha citing a lack of inspiration and merely "going through the motions." "He tried a collaboration with Trent. And that seemed to work well. Rumor is that up to 20 tracks were done, but nothing ever happened. In interviews, Zach said he was just going through the motions and was uninspired by the whole experience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unreleased Projects (Tapeworm, Zach de la Rocha solo album)
xref.body: Trent Reznor has several unreleased projects. The Tapeworm project, formed in 1995 with various collaborators, continued off and on for nine years but never released anything. He also produced around 20 tracks for Zach de la Rocha's solo album after Zach left Rage Against the Machine, which Trent considered "excellent," but Zach felt uncomfortable with the results, and it was never released. "I mean, the tapeworm thing didn't turn out the way it would be to hoped. Worked on Zach's, the deal roaches record, and that went well, but that's never going to see the light of day."

xref.title: Woodstock 99 Performance and Crowd Demeanor
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine was among the "intense and angry new metal bands" featured at Woodstock 99. The presence of such bands contributed to a pervasive atmosphere of "male rage and testosterone" that ultimately fueled the frustration, hatred, and subsequent violence among the festival's 200,000 attendees. "Added in the fact that the lineup was filled with intense and angry new metal bands, LeBiscuit corn, kid rocked, rage guns, the machine, Metallica, tons of mail rage and testosterone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Zack de la Rocha's Political Passion
xref.body: While all members of Rage Against the Machine were political activists, singer Zack de la Rocha was "exponentially more passionate" in that direction, which contributed to internal differences. "While everyone else in the band was political and had definite activist streaks, Zach was exponentially more passionate in that direction."

xref.title: Zack de la Rocha's Project
xref.body: Following his departure from Rage Against the Machine, Zack de la Rocha pursued various solo endeavors and collaborations, including a project named One Day as a Lion. This project has since received attention, indicating de la Rocha's continued musical output beyond his work with Rage. "Zach also has a little project called One Day as a Lion that has received some attention."

xref.title: Zero DB Initiative Signatory
xref.body: Members of Rage Against the Machine are among the artists who signed the Zero DB initiative, formed in 2008 as part of the charity Reprieve. This initiative encourages condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce the Convention Against Torture and other treaties related to the treatment of prisoners. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."
